title: ROMS-IMLE: A Minimalist Approach to Competitive Single-Step Generative Modelling

annotations.label: $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$
annotations.short: $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ is the standard normal prior for the latent codes $\mathbf{z}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{z}_m$.
annotations.details: Appendix D specifies $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{1024}$: each coordinate has mean zero and variance one, and $I$ is the identity covariance. These are generator input latent codes, distinct from the encoded-image latent maps predicted on ImageNet.

annotations.label: $\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$
annotations.short: $\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$ is the standard normal prior for the input latent code $\mathbf{z}$.
annotations.details: Here $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{1024}$ and $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity covariance. The mapping network turns $\mathbf{z}$ into style vector $\mathbf{w}$; the encoded-image latent map predicted on ImageNet is a different representation.

annotations.label: Gaussian
annotations.short: Gaussian noise used as the starting endpoint of the sampler comparison.
annotations.details: The passage does not specify its dimension or covariance. The generator input latent code dimension stated elsewhere should not be transferred to this sampler.

annotations.label: $\argmin$
annotations.short: $\argmin_\theta$ returns a setting of generator parameters $\theta$ that minimizes the objective.
annotations.details: The resulting parameter setting is denoted $\theta_{\text{IMLE}}$. The inner $\min_j$ instead returns a distance for each real example, and the expectation averages over sampled latent-code pools.

annotations.label: $\arg\min$
annotations.short: $\arg\min_j$ selects the index $j$ with the smallest distance to the real target $\mathbf{x}_i$.
annotations.details: Algorithm 1 stores that index as $\sigma(i)$ and uses latent code $\mathbf{z}_{\sigma(i)}$ for optimization. Selection only searches the $m$ sampled candidates, so its best match can still be poor.

annotations.label: $\nabla_\theta$
annotations.short: $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{J}$ is the gradient of the accumulated loss $\mathcal{J}$ with respect to generator parameters $\theta$.
annotations.details: The update $\theta\gets\theta-(\eta/L)\nabla_\theta\mathcal{J}$ takes a step opposite this gradient. Here $\eta$ is the learning rate and $L$ the number of stages, so the loss sum is averaged over stages.

annotations.label: $f_\theta$
annotations.short: The general IMLE generator $f_\theta$ maps a latent code $\mathbf{z}\sim\pi(\mathbf{z})$ to a generated sample $f_\theta(\mathbf{z})$.
annotations.details: Here $\theta$ denotes its trainable parameters and $\pi$ the latent-code prior. Matching compares $f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j)$ with each real example $\mathbf{x}_i$ using $d$. This definition leaves the network architecture general; it does not require the resolution-stage decomposition introduced later.

annotations.label: $f_{\theta^{l}}$
annotations.short: $f_{\theta^l}$ is resolution block $l$, with trainable parameters $\theta^l$.
annotations.details: It follows blocks $1,\ldots,l-1$ in $f_\theta$. A separate output head reads out $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^l$ for comparison with $K_l(\mathbf{x}_i)$; Algorithm 1 suppresses this head in its shorthand for the composed stage output.

annotations.label: $f_{\theta^{L}}$
annotations.short: $f_{\theta^L}$ is the last resolution block in the generator $f_\theta$.
annotations.details: It follows $f_{\theta^{L-1}}$ and produces the final-resolution representation. Its output head gives the final prediction compared with the real target; $L$ counts resolution stages.

annotations.label: $f_{\theta^{L-1}}$
annotations.short: $f_{\theta^{L-1}}$ is the penultimate resolution block of $f_\theta$.
annotations.details: It passes its representation to the final block $f_{\theta^L}$. Its own output head also receives a direct loss against the target downsampled by $K_{L-1}$.

annotations.label: $f_{\theta^{1}}$
annotations.short: $f_{\theta^1}$ is the first, lowest-resolution block in the generator decomposition.
annotations.details: It is applied first in $f_\theta=f_{\theta^L}\circ\cdots\circ f_{\theta^1}$. Appendix D implements the generator with a latent-code mapping network and a learned constant feature map; the displayed composition is a schematic description of its stages.

annotations.label: $\theta$
annotations.short: Trainable parameters $\theta$ of the general IMLE generator $f_\theta$.
annotations.details: After selecting a latent code $\mathbf{z}_{\sigma(i)}$ for each real example $\mathbf{x}_i$, optimization changes $\theta$ to bring $f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_{\sigma(i)})$ closer to $\mathbf{x}_i$. The background objective does not specify a partition of $\theta$ into resolution stages.

annotations.label: $\theta_{\text{IMLE}}$
annotations.short: $\theta_{\text{IMLE}}$ denotes parameters minimizing the expected sum of nearest-candidate distances.
annotations.details: For each real example $\mathbf{x}_i$, the objective takes $\min_{j\in[m]}d(\mathbf{x}_i,f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j))$, where $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. It sums over all $n$ examples and averages over newly sampled latent-code pools. This is the optimization target, not the parameters at a particular iteration.

annotations.label: $\pi(\mathbf{z})$
annotations.short: $\pi(\mathbf{z})$ is the prior distribution of the generator input latent code $\mathbf{z}$.
annotations.details: The background objective allows a general prior. Algorithm 1 instantiates it as $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$, with the 1024-dimensional latent codes specified in Appendix D. The generated output is $f_\theta(\mathbf{z})$.

annotations.label: $p_\mathrm{data}(\mathbf{x})$
annotations.short: $p_\mathrm{data}(\mathbf{x})$ is the distribution of real samples $\mathbf{x}$ that IMLE aims to model.
annotations.details: The training set $\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n$ supplies $n$ examples from this distribution. Learning $f_\theta$ should make its outputs for latent codes drawn from $\pi(\mathbf{z})$ resemble these data.

annotations.label: $p_\mathrm{data}$
annotations.short: $p_\mathrm{data}$ supplies clean real endpoints $\mathbf{x}_0$ for interpolant training.
annotations.details: The objective draws $\mathbf{x}_0\sim p_\mathrm{data}$ and noise $\mathbf{x}_T\sim p_T$, then constructs $\mathbf{x}_t$ using $q_t$. These are the endpoint and intermediate variables in the training comparison.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{x}_i$
annotations.short: Real training example $\mathbf{x}_i$, where $i$ indexes the dataset.
annotations.details: In the IMLE objective, $\mathbf{x}_i$ is compared with generated candidates $f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j)$. The minimum over $j$ gives this example its own nearest-candidate loss, and the sum over $i$ includes every real example.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{z}_j$
annotations.short: Latent code $\mathbf{z}_j$ sampled from the prior for candidate $j$.
annotations.details: The generator turns it into $f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j)$. Matching compares this output with real examples $\mathbf{x}_i$ across the pool of $m$ sampled latent codes; $j$ indexes candidates, not coordinates of the latent vector.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{z}_{\sigma(i)}$
annotations.short: Latent code $\mathbf{z}_{\sigma(i)}$ whose generated output was selected for real example $\mathbf{x}_i$.
annotations.details: The index $\sigma(i)$ is chosen by nearest-neighbour matching. The same selected latent code is used for every stage output $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l$ while $\theta$ is optimized; the assignment is recomputed in a later matching round.

annotations.label: $\sigma(i)$
annotations.short: $\sigma(i)$ is the candidate index selected to match real example $\mathbf{x}_i$.
annotations.details: Algorithm 1 sets $\sigma(i)=\arg\min_{j\in[m]}d(\mathbf{x}_i,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j)$, where $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j=f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j)$. Different real examples may select the same candidate; this is not a one-to-one assignment.

annotations.label: $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^{l}$
annotations.short: $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l$ is the stage-$l$ prediction generated from the latent code matched to $\mathbf{x}_i$.
annotations.details: The stage loss compares it with $K_l(\mathbf{x}_i)$, the real target at the same resolution. All stages use the same assignment $\sigma(i)$, chosen using final outputs. For ImageNet, Appendix D specifies that real images are encoded before downsampling, and predictions are latent maps.

annotations.label: $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j$
annotations.short: $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j=f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j)$ is the final output generated from latent code $\mathbf{z}_j$.
annotations.details: The matching step compares $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j$ with each real target $\mathbf{x}_i$ to choose $\sigma(i)$. It is an image for pixel-space models and an encoded-image latent map for the ImageNet model.

annotations.label: $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{l}$
annotations.short: $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^l$ is the prediction read out at resolution stage $l$ of $f_\theta$.
annotations.details: A stage-specific output head converts stage features into a prediction comparable with $K_l(\mathbf{x}_i)$, the target at the same resolution. Every stage $l=1,\ldots,L$, including the final stage, receives a direct training loss. For ImageNet, the predictions and targets are encoded-image latent maps.

annotations.label: $K_l$
annotations.short: $K_l$ downsamples a real target to the spatial resolution of stage $l$.
annotations.details: The loss compares $K_l(\mathbf{x}_i)$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l$, the prediction for the matched latent code. Appendix D uses bicubic resizing; for ImageNet it first encodes the real image and then applies $K_l$ to that latent map.

annotations.label: $d(\cdot, \cdot)$
annotations.short: $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ — abstract comparison function supplied to the training pseudocode.
annotations.details: The pseudocode uses one letter for selection and optimization. Appendix D specifies different concrete comparisons for these operations; follow the annotation on the corresponding step. The optimization comparison is averaged over its elements.

annotations.label: $d(\cdot,\cdot)$
annotations.short: $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ — distance between a real example and a generated candidate.
annotations.details: The abstract objective leaves this choice open. The appendix distinguishes the metric used to choose a candidate from the loss used for parameter optimization.

annotations.label: $\mathcal{J}$
annotations.short: $\mathcal{J}$ accumulates the minibatch mean loss at each of the $L$ generator stages.
annotations.details: After the loop, $\mathcal{J}=\sum_{l=1}^L\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}d(K_l(\mathbf{x}_i),\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l)$. Here $S$ is the minibatch index set and $|S|$ its size. The update uses $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{J}/L$, so it optimizes the mean across stages.

annotations.label: $\eta$
annotations.short: $\eta$ sets the step size for updating generator parameters $\theta$.
annotations.details: Algorithm 1 uses $\theta\gets\theta-(\eta/L)\nabla_\theta\mathcal{J}$, where $\mathcal{J}$ sums stage losses and $L$ counts stages. Dividing by $L$ turns that sum into a stage average.

annotations.label: $m/n$
annotations.short: $m/n$ is the ratio of generated matching candidates to real training examples.
annotations.details: The pool has $m$ candidates shared across $n$ real examples, rather than a separate pool for each example. Larger $m/n$ can improve nearest matches but costs more generation and search work. Main experiments use $m/n=5$.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{x}_0$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{x}_0\sim p_\mathrm{data}$ is a clean real sample used as the data endpoint during interpolant training.
annotations.details: Together with noise endpoint $\mathbf{x}_T$, it defines the conditional law $q_t(\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_T)$ of training state $\mathbf{x}_t$. The generated clean endpoint is instead written $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0$.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{x}_T$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{x}_T\sim p_T$ is the noise endpoint at time $T$.
annotations.details: During training it is paired with real endpoint $\mathbf{x}_0$ to construct $\mathbf{x}_t$. During sampling it is the starting input to $g^T_\theta$ in the chain that produces $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0$.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{x}_t$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{x}_t$ is a training state drawn from $q_t(\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_T)$ at time $t$.
annotations.details: The model prediction $g^t_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t)$ is compared with target $g^t(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_t)$. This state comes from the prescribed interpolation law; $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_t$ instead denotes a state produced during sampling.

annotations.label: $q_t(\mathbf{x}_t \vert \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_T)$
annotations.short: $q_t(\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_T)$ specifies the training-state distribution given clean and noise endpoints.
annotations.details: At time $t$, it constructs intermediate state $\mathbf{x}_t$ from real example $\mathbf{x}_0$ and noise $\mathbf{x}_T$. The manuscript leaves this law general, so no particular interpolation formula or density can be inferred.

annotations.label: $q_t$
annotations.short: $q_t$ denotes the conditional law $q_t(\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_T)$ for intermediate training states.
annotations.details: The endpoints are clean data $\mathbf{x}_0\sim p_\mathrm{data}$ and noise $\mathbf{x}_T\sim p_T$. The paper does not fix a universal density or interpolation formula for $q_t$.

annotations.label: $p_T$
annotations.short: $p_T$ is the distribution of noise endpoint $\mathbf{x}_T$.
annotations.details: Training draws $\mathbf{x}_T\sim p_T$ to construct interpolated states, and sampling starts from the same endpoint distribution. This is distinct from $\pi(\mathbf{z})$, the latent-code prior for the IMLE generator.

annotations.label: $p_{T}$
annotations.short: $p_T$ is the distribution of noise endpoint $\mathbf{x}_T$.
annotations.details: Training draws $\mathbf{x}_T\sim p_T$ to construct interpolated states, and sampling starts from the same endpoint distribution. This is distinct from $\pi(\mathbf{z})$, the latent-code prior for the IMLE generator.

annotations.label: $\mathcal{L}$
annotations.short: $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ averages the discrepancy between prediction $g^t_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t)$ and target $g^t(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_t)$.
annotations.details: The comparison is $\ell_t$, evaluated at a sampled time $t$, real endpoint $\mathbf{x}_0$, noise endpoint $\mathbf{x}_T$, and conditional training state $\mathbf{x}_t$. Thus supervision is defined along training interpolations, not by rolling out generated trajectories.

annotations.label: $\tilde{\mathcal{L}}$
annotations.short: $\tilde{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)$ averages the interpolant training loss over integer times $t=1,\ldots,T$.
annotations.details: Each term compares $g^t_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t)$ with $g^t(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_t)$ using $\ell_t$. The factor $1/T$ gives equal weight to the $T$ time stages; this motivates the later average over $L$ generator resolutions.

annotations.label: $\ell_t$
annotations.short: $\ell_t$ compares target $g^t(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_t)$ with prediction $g^t_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t)$ at time $t$.
annotations.details: The manuscript leaves this comparison general. The subscript $t$ allows its form or weighting to depend on interpolation time; it is not the generator-stage loss $d$ introduced later.

annotations.label: $g^t$
annotations.short: $g^t(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_t)$ is the desired training output at time $t$.
annotations.details: It is constructed from clean example $\mathbf{x}_0$ and interpolation state $\mathbf{x}_t$ and is compared with learned prediction $g^t_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t)$. Its output type is left general; the superscript $t$ indexes time, not a power.

annotations.label: $g^t_{\theta}$
annotations.short: $g^t_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t)$ is the learned prediction at training state $\mathbf{x}_t$ and time $t$.
annotations.details: The loss $\ell_t$ compares it with target $g^t(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_t)$. Here $\theta$ is the predictor parameter set. Later the manuscript schematically reuses $g^t_\theta$ for an entire sampler update; that is a different local role.

annotations.label: $g^1_{\theta}$
annotations.short: $g^1_\theta$ is the last update applied in the unrolled sampler.
annotations.details: $g^1_\theta(\mathbf{\hat{x}}_1)=\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0$ produces the final clean sample. Composition is evaluated from right to left in $h_\theta=g^1_\theta\circ\cdots\circ g^T_\theta$.

annotations.label: $g^2_{\theta}$
annotations.short: $g^2_\theta$ is the penultimate update applied in the unrolled sampler.
annotations.details: $g^2_\theta(\mathbf{\hat{x}}_2)=\mathbf{\hat{x}}_1$ supplies the input to final update $g^1_\theta$. Composition is evaluated from right to left in $h_\theta=g^1_\theta\circ\cdots\circ g^T_\theta$.

annotations.label: $g^T_{\theta}$
annotations.short: $g^T_\theta$ is the first update applied in the unrolled sampler.
annotations.details: $g^T_\theta(\mathbf{x}_T)=\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{T-1}$ begins at the prior-noise draw $\mathbf{x}_T$. Composition is evaluated from right to left in $h_\theta=g^1_\theta\circ\cdots\circ g^T_\theta$.

annotations.label: $h_{\theta}$
annotations.short: $h_\theta$ maps noise $\mathbf{x}_T$ to generated sample $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0$ by composing all sampler updates.
annotations.details: The definition is $h_\theta=g^1_\theta\circ\cdots\circ g^T_\theta$, with $g^T_\theta$ applied first. Calling the chain one model regroups its $T$ updates; it does not reduce them to one denoising-network evaluation.

annotations.label: $h_\theta$
annotations.short: $h_\theta$ maps noise $\mathbf{x}_T$ to generated sample $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0$ by composing all sampler updates.
annotations.details: The definition is $h_\theta=g^1_\theta\circ\cdots\circ g^T_\theta$, with $g^T_\theta$ applied first. Calling the chain one model regroups its $T$ updates; it does not reduce them to one denoising-network evaluation.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0=h_\theta(\mathbf{x}_T)$ is the final sample produced from noise endpoint $\mathbf{x}_T$.
annotations.details: The hat distinguishes a generated sample from real clean example $\mathbf{x}_0$. It is produced after the last update $g^1_\theta$ of the unrolled sampler.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{t-1}$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{t-1}=g^t_\theta(\mathbf{\hat{x}}_t)$ is the generated state after the time-$t$ sampler update.
annotations.details: For $t>1$, it becomes input to the next update $g^{t-1}_\theta$; at $t=1$, it is the final generated sample $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_0$. The index change alone does not guarantee a decrease in image error.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_t$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_t$ is the generated input state to sampler update $g^t_\theta$.
annotations.details: The update produces $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{t-1}$. At the start, $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_T$ corresponds to the noise draw $\mathbf{x}_T$; interior states come from preceding updates rather than the training law $q_t$.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{w}$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{w}$ is the style vector obtained by mapping the input latent code $\mathbf{z}$ through the mapping network.
annotations.details: Whereas $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{1024}$ is sampled from the prior, $\mathbf{w}$ is a learned transformation of that sample. It supplies the scale and shift controls used by adaptive instance normalization in the decoder layers; the manuscript does not state its dimension.

annotations.label: multi-stage supervision
annotations.short: Each stage prediction $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l$ receives a direct loss against the resolution-matched target $K_l(\mathbf{x}_i)$.
annotations.details: Here $l$ indexes resolution stages and $\sigma(i)$ selects the latent code matched to real example $\mathbf{x}_i$. Losses are averaged over elements, minibatch examples, and stages. Intermediate heads supply training supervision; sampling still evaluates $f_\theta$ in one forward pass.

annotations.label: round-trip rejection
annotations.short: A generated image is rejected if its LPIPS distance from its encode-decode reconstruction exceeds a threshold.
annotations.details: For clarity, write $E$ and $D$ for the frozen image encoder and decoder, and $\mathbf{y}$ for a generated image. The compared images are $\mathbf{y}$ and $D(E(\mathbf{y}))$. Appendix D reports that the fixed threshold rejects roughly 5% of candidates; its numerical value is not given. This adds encoder/decoder work beyond the generator evaluation.

annotations.label: Geman-McClure
annotations.short: The robust penalty selected by the paper to reduce the influence of mismatched pairs.
annotations.details: Configuration E uses this penalty with direct intermediate supervision and has the best FID in the Oxford Flowers loss ablation. Its scale and full implementation are not specified in the manuscript.

annotations.label: Cauchy
annotations.short: One of the robust loss candidates in the ablation.
annotations.details: Configuration C replaces the loss of the multi-stage baseline with this penalty. The manuscript does not give its scale parameter.

annotations.label: Pseudo-Huber
annotations.short: A smooth robust alternative to squared error, tested in the loss ablation.
annotations.details: Configuration D tests this penalty in place of the loss of the multi-stage baseline. The manuscript does not give its scale parameter.

annotations.label: $\theta$
annotations.short: $\theta$ — parameters of the time-dependent denoising model.
annotations.details: The same model parameters are shared across time-conditioned stages in the unrolled comparison; these are distinct from the parameters of the proposed generator.

annotations.label: $p(\mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}_{T})$
annotations.short: $p(\mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}_{T})$ — conditional distribution of the final clean endpoint given the initial noisy endpoint.
annotations.details: Integrating over all intermediate states expresses the entire reverse chain as a single endpoint conditional.

annotations.label: $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{0} \mid \mathbf{x}_{1})$
annotations.short: $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{0} \mid \mathbf{x}_{1})$ — final reverse transition from state 1 to the clean endpoint.
annotations.details: This is the last factor applied in sampling, although it appears first in the product as written.

annotations.label: $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{1} \mid \mathbf{x}_{2})$
annotations.short: $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{1} \mid \mathbf{x}_{2})$ — reverse transition from state 2 to state 1.
annotations.details: Its conditioning state differs from the final clean-endpoint transition.

annotations.label: $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{T-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_{T})$
annotations.short: $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{T-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_{T})$ — first reverse transition from the prior endpoint.
annotations.details: Sampling this conditional begins the reverse chain at the noisiest end.

annotations.label: $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_t)$
annotations.short: General reverse-step conditional from time $t$ to time $t-1$.
annotations.details: The product combines these factors; integration marginalizes every intermediate state to obtain the endpoint conditional.

annotations.label: Gaussian
annotations.short: FID approximates each feature distribution by a multivariate normal with fitted mean and covariance.
annotations.details: This is an evaluation approximation and differs from the zero-mean, identity-covariance prior sampled by the generator.

annotations.label: $[m]$
annotations.short: Indices of the $m$ generated candidates in the current matching pool.
annotations.details: The notation denotes the integer set $\{1,\ldots,m\}$. The nearest candidate is selected from this finite pool.

annotations.label: $[n]$
annotations.short: Indices of all $n$ real training examples.
annotations.details: The notation denotes $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A minibatch is a subset of these indices.

annotations.label: $[L]$
annotations.short: Indices of the $L$ generator resolution stages.
annotations.details: The notation denotes $\{1,\ldots,L\}$. Every stage receives direct supervision.

annotations.label: $n$
annotations.short: $n$ — number of real examples in the training dataset.
annotations.details: Each example contributes its nearest-candidate loss to the objective.

annotations.label: $m$
annotations.short: $m$ — number of generated candidates used in a matching round.
annotations.details: The ratio to the number of real examples controls the sampling budget and nearest-neighbour search workload.

annotations.label: $t$
annotations.short: $t$ — outer matching-and-optimization round in Algorithm 1.
annotations.details: This is a training iteration index, distinct from the interpolation time denoted by the same letter in the background section.

annotations.label: $T$
annotations.short: $T$ — number of outer training rounds in Algorithm 1.
annotations.details: This algorithmic stopping count is distinct from the noise-endpoint time or sampler depth used in the interpolant comparison.

annotations.label: $S$
annotations.short: $S\subseteq[n]$ contains the real-example indices in the current optimization minibatch.
annotations.details: Here $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $|S|$ is the minibatch size. Each $i\in S$ uses the matched latent code $\mathbf{z}_{\sigma(i)}$ at all stages, and $|S|^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}$ averages their losses.

annotations.label: $d$
annotations.short: $d(\mathbf{x}_i,f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j))$ measures how far candidate $j$ is from real example $i$.
annotations.details: The inner minimum chooses the smallest of these distances for each $\mathbf{x}_i$; the outer sum includes every real example. This general IMLE objective leaves the comparison function unspecified.

annotations.label: $d$
annotations.short: $d(\mathbf{x}_i,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j)$ is the selection distance used to choose the matched candidate index $\sigma(i)$.
annotations.details: Appendix D uses LPIPS between images for pixel models and squared Euclidean distance between real and generated EQ-VAE latent maps for ImageNet. After selection, optimization uses the separate per-stage training loss also denoted $d$ in Algorithm 1.

annotations.label: $g^t_{\theta}$
annotations.short: Here $g^t_\theta$ maps generated state $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_t$ to $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{t-1}$.
annotations.details: The sampler is written schematically as $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{t-1}=g^t_\theta(\mathbf{\hat{x}}_t)$. This use denotes the whole update; a concrete sampler may combine the trained prediction with a numerical update rule. The same glyph in the training loss denotes a prediction evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_t$.

annotations.label: $d$
annotations.short: $d(K_l(\mathbf{x}_i),\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l)$ penalizes the difference between the stage-$l$ target and matched prediction.
annotations.details: ImageNet training averages Geman-McClure penalties on elementwise latent-map residuals. Pixel training combines LPIPS, DINO, and pixel losses with weights 1.0, 1.0, and 0.1. The manuscript does not fully specify how robustification interacts with those pixel-loss components.

annotations.label: $d(\cdot, \cdot)$
annotations.short: $d(\mathbf{x}_i,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j)$ is the selection distance used to choose the matched candidate index $\sigma(i)$.
annotations.details: Appendix D uses LPIPS between images for pixel models and squared Euclidean distance between real and generated EQ-VAE latent maps for ImageNet. After selection, optimization uses the separate per-stage training loss also denoted $d$ in Algorithm 1.

annotations.label: $d(\cdot, \cdot)$
annotations.short: Here $d$ is the optimization penalty applied to a prediction and its matched real target.
annotations.details: Replacing it with a robust loss reduces the gradient contribution of large mismatches in $d(K_l(\mathbf{x}_i),\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l)$. Appendix D separately specifies the distance that selects $\sigma(i)$; this paragraph does not establish that selection uses the same robust penalty.

annotations.label: $L$
annotations.short: $L$ — number of generator resolution stages.
annotations.details: The training procedure directly supervises every stage and averages the accumulated loss over this count.

annotations.label: $l$
annotations.short: $l$ — generator resolution-stage index.
annotations.details: It increases from the first, lowest-resolution stage toward the final output stage; it is distinct from interpolation time in the sampler comparison.

annotations.label: $|S|$
annotations.short: $|S|$ — number of real examples in the current minibatch.
annotations.details: Dividing the summed example losses by this count forms a minibatch mean before averaging across stages.

annotations.label: $t$
annotations.short: $t$ — interpolation time in the noise-to-data comparison.
annotations.details: Training samples a continuous time in Equation 2; the reformulation in Equation 4 sums over integer times. Neither use is an outer generator-training round.

annotations.label: $T$
annotations.short: $T$ — noise-endpoint time and, in the discrete unrolled view, total number of sampler stages.
annotations.details: The paper moves from a continuous-time interval to stages numbered 1 through this endpoint. This use is separate from the stopping count in Algorithm 1.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{z}$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{z}$ is the generator input latent code, sampled as $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$.
annotations.details: Appendix D specifies $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{1024}$. The mapping network transforms it into style vector $\mathbf{w}$, which controls the decoder. It differs from the encoded-image latent map generated by the ImageNet model.

annotations.label: $k$
annotations.short: $k$ — neighbour count determining feature-space neighbourhood radii for precision and recall.
annotations.details: Appendix E sets this count to three. Changing it changes the estimated sets used for fidelity and coverage measurements.

annotations.label: precision
annotations.short: Precision is the fraction of generated samples whose features fall in neighbourhoods of real-data features.
annotations.details: Higher precision indicates more realistic generated samples under the chosen feature representation. Appendix E constructs neighbourhood radii using $k=3$ nearest neighbours in image-feature space.

annotations.label: recall
annotations.short: Recall is the fraction of real samples whose features fall in neighbourhoods of generated-sample features.
annotations.details: Higher recall indicates that generated samples cover more of the real-data variation under the chosen feature representation. Appendix E constructs neighbourhood radii using $k=3$ nearest neighbours in image-feature space.

annotations.label: ROMS-IMLE
annotations.short: The paper's robust multi-stage version of IMLE.
annotations.details: It combines direct supervision at every generator resolution with a robust optimization loss. Round-trip rejection is an additional inference-time option for the latent-space model.

annotations.label: $\theta^{1}$
annotations.short: Trainable parameters belonging to generator stage $1$.
annotations.details: This is one component of the full parameter tuple. It controls this resolution stage rather than the entire generator.

annotations.label: $\theta^{L}$
annotations.short: Trainable parameters belonging to generator stage $L$.
annotations.details: This is one component of the full parameter tuple. It controls this resolution stage rather than the entire generator.

annotations.label: $\min$
annotations.short: $\min_{j\in[m]}$ returns the smallest candidate distance for real example $\mathbf{x}_i$.
annotations.details: The compared values are $d(\mathbf{x}_i,f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j))$ for $j\in[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. This returns a distance, whereas the later matching step stores the minimizing index as $\sigma(i)$.

annotations.label: $f_\theta$
annotations.short: The ROMS generator $f_\theta$ maps latent code $\mathbf{z}$ to its output through $L$ resolution stages.
annotations.details: Here the chosen architecture is written $f_\theta=f_{\theta^L}\circ\cdots\circ f_{\theta^1}$, where $\theta=(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^L)$ collects stage parameters. Intermediate predictions $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^l$ receive direct training losses; generation follows one forward pass. Outputs are images for pixel models and encoded-image latent maps for ImageNet.

annotations.label: $\theta$
annotations.short: $\theta=(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^L)$ collects the trainable parameters of the generator stages.
annotations.details: The stage parameters $\theta^l$ belong to block $f_{\theta^l}$. Algorithm 1 updates the full tuple using $\theta\gets\theta-(\eta/L)\nabla_\theta\mathcal{J}$, where $\eta$ is the learning rate and $\mathcal{J}$ sums minibatch mean stage losses.

annotations.label: $\mathbf{x}_i$
annotations.short: $\mathbf{x}_i$ is the real example that supplies the stage targets for its matched latent code.
annotations.details: For each stage $l$, prediction $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\sigma(i)}^l$ is compared with $K_l(\mathbf{x}_i)$. Appendix D clarifies the ImageNet shorthand: the real image is first encoded with the frozen encoder, and its latent map is then downsampled.

IMLE.label: Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation
IMLE.short: Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (IMLE) trains a generator $f_\theta$ by matching every real example $\mathbf{x}_i$ to a nearby generated sample $f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j)$.
IMLE.details: Draw $m$ latent codes $\mathbf{z}_j$ from prior $\pi$, then choose $\sigma(i)=\arg\min_{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}}d(\mathbf{x}_i,f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_j))$ for each real example $i$. Here $d$ is a distance and $\sigma(i)$ the selected index. Hold these assignments while updating parameters $\theta$ to reduce the matched distances, then resample and repeat. Every real example contributes a loss, encouraging coverage. At generation time, draw a fresh latent code $\mathbf{z}\sim\pi$ and evaluate $f_\theta(\mathbf{z})$. The original IMLE result relates this objective to maximum likelihood under stated conditions; arbitrary distances do not automatically give exact maximum likelihood.

FID.label: Fréchet Inception Distance
FID.short: FID compares the means and covariances of real and generated image features; lower values are better.
FID.details: It summarizes distributional similarity in a pretrained image feature space. It does not independently measure sample fidelity and coverage, and comparisons depend on the feature extractor and evaluation protocol. The paper evaluates with 50,000 generated images.

Normal.label: Standard multivariate normal distribution
Normal.short: A continuous distribution on $\mathbb{R}^D$ with zero mean and identity covariance.
Normal.details: For latent vector $\mathbf{z}=(z_1,\ldots,z_D)$, the density is $p(\mathbf{z})=(2\pi)^{-D/2}\exp(-\sum_{k=1}^D z_k^2/2)$ on $\mathbb{R}^D$. Here $D$ is the dimension, $k$ indexes coordinates, and $\pi$ is the circle constant, distinct from the prior-distribution symbol. Coordinates are independent with mean zero and variance one; $\mathbf{I}$ denotes identity covariance.

Uniform.label: Continuous uniform distribution
Uniform.short: A continuous distribution assigning equal density to every point in a finite interval.
Uniform.details: On $(0,T]$ with endpoint $T>0$, the density is $p(t)=1/T$ for $0<t\le T$ and zero elsewhere. Equal-length subintervals have equal probability. The time variable $t$ here is an interpolation time, not an outer optimization round.

Expectation.label: Expectation
Expectation.short: An expectation averages a quantity over the random variables named below the operator.
Expectation.details: For a discrete variable, the expectation is the sum of each value times its probability; for a continuous variable, it is the integral of the value times its density. Training approximates such averages using sampled examples.

Argmin.label: Argument of the minimum
Argmin.short: The argument of the minimum returns an input or index attaining the smallest objective value.
Argmin.details: Unlike a minimum, which is a value, an argument of the minimum identifies where that value occurs. Here it selects either model parameters or the nearest generated candidate, depending on its subscript.

Composition.label: Function composition
Composition.short: Composition applies the rightmost function first and passes its output to the next function.
Composition.details: For functions $a$ and $b$, $(a\circ b)(z)=a(b(z))$. A stack of distinct network blocks can therefore be one forward pass even though it contains several composed transformations.

Gradient.label: Gradient
Gradient.short: A gradient collects partial derivatives of a scalar loss with respect to the variable being changed.
Gradient.details: For loss $\mathcal{J}$ and parameters $\theta$, $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{J}$ guides the parameter update. A gradient can instead be taken with respect to a generated sample: for residual vector $\mathbf{r}$, squared error has derivative $\nabla_{\mathbf{r}}\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2=2\mathbf{r}$. This explains why large mismatches can dominate training.

Robust.label: Robust loss
Robust.short: A robust loss limits the influence of unusually large residuals on parameter updates.
Robust.details: A residual is a prediction minus its target. Squared error gives large residuals proportionally large gradients; the paper replaces it with less rapidly growing penalties to reduce damage from accidental poor matches.

LPIPS.label: Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity
LPIPS.short: LPIPS compares images through learned visual features instead of raw pixel differences alone.
LPIPS.details: The paper uses it for pixel-space nearest-neighbour selection, as one term in pixel-space optimization, and to measure the image round-trip reconstruction cost. These are distinct uses of the same perceptual comparison.

GaussianFeatures.label: Multivariate normal distribution
GaussianFeatures.short: A continuous distribution on a real vector space, parameterized by its mean and covariance.
GaussianFeatures.details: For a vector $x$ with $D$ real coordinates, mean vector $\mu$, and positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$, the density on $\mathbb{R}^D$ is $(2\pi)^{-D/2}|\Sigma|^{-1/2}\exp[-(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)/2]$. Here $\pi$ is the circle constant. The mean sets the center; the covariance sets the spread and dependence between coordinates.

ExponentialFunction.label: Exponential function
ExponentialFunction.short: $\exp(u)=e^u$ is the exponential function; $e$ is Euler's number.
ExponentialFunction.details: The real input $u$ is dimensionless. The function is positive, equals one at zero, and is its own derivative. In a normal density it turns a negative squared distance into a positive density factor.

MatrixNotation.label: Matrix notation in normal densities
MatrixNotation.short: A covariance matrix records variances on its diagonal and pairwise covariances elsewhere.
MatrixNotation.details: $I$ is the identity matrix. For a covariance matrix $\Sigma$, $|\Sigma|$ is its determinant and $\Sigma^{-1}$ its inverse; $v^\top$ transposes a column vector $v$. Positive definiteness means $v^\top\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v$, ensuring an ordinary full-dimensional normal density exists.

GemanMcClure.label: Geman-McClure loss
GemanMcClure.short: Geman-McClure is a bounded residual penalty: sufficiently large errors have decreasing influence on the update.
GemanMcClure.details: A standard form is $\rho(r)=r^2/(r^2+c^2)$, where $r$ is one prediction-minus-target residual and $c>0$ is a scale. Its derivative $\rho^{\prime}(r)=2rc^2/(r^2+c^2)^2$ tends to zero for large $|r|$. Normalizations vary; ROMS-IMLE does not specify its exact scale or normalization.

CauchyLoss.label: Cauchy loss
CauchyLoss.short: A robust residual penalty with logarithmic growth for large errors.
CauchyLoss.details: A standard form is $\rho(r)=c^2\log(1+(r/c)^2)$, with residual $r$ and scale $c>0$. Its derivative $2r/(1+(r/c)^2)$ decreases in magnitude for sufficiently large $|r|$. This describes a loss, not a specified residual distribution; the manuscript does not give its scale or normalization.

PseudoHuber.label: Pseudo-Huber loss
PseudoHuber.short: A smooth robust penalty that is approximately quadratic near zero and linear for large errors.
PseudoHuber.details: A standard form is $\rho(r)=c^2(\sqrt{1+(r/c)^2}-1)$, where $r$ is a residual and $c>0$ a scale. Its derivative $r/\sqrt{1+(r/c)^2}$ approaches magnitude $c$ for large errors. Thus large-error influence is bounded, rather than vanishing; the manuscript does not give the scale.

AdaIN.label: Adaptive Instance Normalization
AdaIN.short: AdaIN normalizes each feature channel and applies style-dependent scale and shift.
AdaIN.details: It lets a style representation control channel statistics. In this generator, the mapped input latent code supplies the style information used to modulate the decoder.

DINO.label: Self-distillation with no labels
DINO.short: DINO learns visual representations by training a student to match a teacher on different views of an image without class labels.
DINO.details: The teacher is updated from the student during representation learning. Here DINO supplies pretrained image features for a training-loss component; its original representation-learning objective is distinct from the generator loss.

EQVAE.label: EQ-VAE
EQVAE.short: An image encoder-decoder whose latent space is regularized for consistency under image transformations.
EQVAE.details: The cited model improves the structure of encoded image representations. ROMS-IMLE keeps it frozen, generates maps in its latent space, and decodes those maps into images. These maps differ from the random latent codes fed into the generator.

SI.label: Stochastic interpolant
SI.short: A stochastic interpolant defines random intermediate states $\mathbf{x}_t$ between clean endpoint $\mathbf{x}_0$ and noise endpoint $\mathbf{x}_T$.
SI.details: The paper writes their conditional law as $q_t(\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_T)$, where $t$ indexes interpolation time. It groups diffusion and flow matching under this framework. Training supervises predictions at intermediate states; the proposed generator transfers that idea to resolution index $l$, using targets $K_l(\mathbf{x}_i)$ for real example $\mathbf{x}_i$.

NFE.label: Number of function evaluations
NFE.short: NFE counts generator or denoising-model evaluations for a candidate sample under the reported sampling procedure.
NFE.details: It is not a count of neural layers or a complete compute budget. Encoder/decoder work and discarded candidates can add cost beyond the one generator evaluation reported for a ROMS-IMLE candidate.

PrecisionRecall.label: Generative precision and recall
PrecisionRecall.short: Precision estimates generated-sample fidelity; recall estimates coverage of real-data variation.
PrecisionRecall.details: Neighbourhoods around feature vectors approximate the sets occupied by each distribution. Precision is the fraction of generated features within real-data neighbourhoods; recall is the fraction of real features within generated-data neighbourhoods. Both lie between zero and one; results depend on the feature extractor and neighbourhood size.

L2.label: Euclidean norm
L2.short: For a residual vector $\mathbf{r}=(r_1,\ldots,r_D)$, the Euclidean norm is $\|\mathbf{r}\|_2=(\sum_{k=1}^D r_k^2)^{1/2}$.
L2.details: Here $D$ counts coordinates and $k$ indexes them. Squared distance is $\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2=\sum_k r_k^2$; its gradient is $2\mathbf{r}$. The unsquared norm has gradient $\mathbf{r}/\|\mathbf{r}\|_2$ for nonzero $\mathbf{r}$. Averaging squared residuals additionally divides by $D$.

Bicubic.label: Bicubic interpolation
Bicubic.short: Bicubic interpolation estimates values on a resized two-dimensional grid using local cubic interpolation.
Bicubic.details: It supplies lower-resolution image or latent targets here. Exact boundary handling and sampling conventions depend on the implementation; the appendix specifies the default PyTorch resizing implementation.

IID.label: Independent and identically distributed
IID.short: The samples are independent draws from the same distribution.
IID.details: Independence means one draw does not change the probabilities for another. The common distribution in the training algorithm is the standard normal input latent code prior.

Minimum.label: Minimum
Minimum.short: A minimum is the smallest value in the set being compared.
Minimum.details: It returns a value rather than the index or input at which that value occurs. In the nearest-candidate objective the minimum is taken over a finite pool.
